rv.q: The new piece promptly establishes itself as magnificent at its first outing in a production by Patrick Marber.
Leopoldstadt is more about love than hate, which is its ultimate triumph.
An early contender for play of the year, it’s not perfect: but how refreshing to see a show with too much, rather than too little, to say.
Ultimately, ‘Leopoldstadt’ is a powerful and sincere tribute to a vanished people.
“Leopoldstadt” demands, with gravity and eloquence, that we never let those visions disappear.
It lives with you long after the curtain has gone down.
And it is deeply, achingly moving.
Patrick Marber’s production teems with life and, indeed, children.
Most vitally, Patrick Marber’s production strongly suggests the cat’s cradle of these relationships.
For all its clunks and flaws, this, like all Stoppard’s plays, in the end comes across as a benign, enriching gift.
For all its debate and distance, this particular family portrait leaves us bereft at history.
Leopoldstadt is a sprawling, noble tribute to families such as the Strausslers.
The result is a multi-generational saga which, for all its opulent staging, becomes faintly generic.
Leopoldstadt is further proof of Sir Tom Stoppard’s unique place in British theatre, the script superbly enhanced by the efforts of Patrick Marber and his cast.
Leopoldstadt tells a rending cross-generational story that looks likely to resound directly with playgoers.

This is a powerful, important new play from one of our greatest living playwrights that, should it prove to be his swansong, means he has gone out on a significant high, even as he dramatises a low point on world history.
Stoppard plays a correct and theatrically brave note; one from which you will need to compose yourself afterwards.
It’s pretty stodgy stuff — a thick soup of declamatory speeches and little potted history lessons, even as events hurtle towards inevitable catastrophe.
